Argentina's Congress Passes Law Restricting Central Bank Printing of Money
articles.summary: The new law aims to prevent the central bank from being used to finance government spending and instead focuses on maintaining the stability of the peso.
articles.content: Argentina's Congress has made a bold move by passing a law that restricts the central bank from printing money to cover government expenses. This significant change is part of President Javier Milei's efforts to tackle the country's long-standing inflation problem. The new legislation aims to prevent the central bank from being used as a means for the government to finance its spending. Milei, a libertarian economist, has been advocating for a more controlled monetary policy to preserve the value of the peso. Despite his pre-election promise to abolish the central bank and replace the local currency with the US dollar, he has continued to pursue this goal in office. The central bank's primary mission will now be focused on maintaining the stability of the peso. The 141-0 vote in favor of the law, with 99 abstentions, is a clear indication of Congress' support for Milei's economic policies. This move comes at a critical time, as preliminary figures suggest that Argentina may have entered recession just months before the presidential election. The country's economy has been plagued by high inflation and currency crises for decades. The new law marks a significant departure from the past practice of printing money to fill the government's financial gap. According to Milei's office, this change brings an end to "91 years of plunder, expropriation, impunity and institutional decay". The impact of this legislation on Argentina's economy remains to be seen, but it is clear that President Milei is committed to implementing far-reaching reforms. The new legislation passed by Congress has imposed significant restrictions on the central bank's lending practices. Specifically, it bars the bank from providing loans to any level of government or otherwise financing government spending. This move is part of President Milei's broader effort to curb unbridled government spending and reduce Argentina's fiscal deficits. However, the final version of the law does not grant the president as much authority over the central bank's leadership as he had initially sought. The original bill would have required a two-thirds majority in both houses of Congress to remove the bank's governor, but this clause was watered down by the Senate and ultimately failed to gain traction in the lower house. Milei's administration has taken steps to rein in public spending in recent years, achieving a surplus where chronic fiscal deficits once prevailed. This shift is also reflected in Argentina's inflation rate, which plummeted from nearly 300% at the start of 2024 to 33% last month. The new charter maintains currency controls within the central bank's purview and sets no clear guidelines for responding to inflationary pressures. As a result, President Milei will retain some degree of control over Argentina's exchange rate, rather than allowing market forces to dictate its value. Argentina's economy has been struggling in recent months, with an estimated 1.8% contraction in the third quarter following a 0.6% decline in the second. This two-quarter downturn is typically considered a recession according to official data released on Tuesday. The peso has remained strong due to tight monetary policy, making Argentine goods expensive abroad at a time when factories are facing a surge of cheaper imports. Meanwhile, oil and gas exports have seen significant growth, but labor-intensive sectors like manufacturing, retail, and construction continue to struggle. Investors are increasingly concerned about Argentina's debt default history, with nine instances of non-payment on record. This has led to a sharp increase in the premium demanded for holding Argentine bonds, as measured by JPMorgan, which more than doubled since early August. The Senate recently approved a bill proposed by President Milei to suspend mandatory primaries, arguing that these contests waste public funds and should be run independently by parties. The legislation now awaits a vote in the lower house, under pressure from the government to pass it before next year's presidential election. The Argentine government is exerting pressure on lawmakers in the lower house to pass legislation that would suspend primary elections, a move seen as crucial for President Javier Milei's chances of re-election. Peronist leaders have expressed strong opposition to this proposal, which would force them to either negotiate behind closed doors or organize a separate primary election. Governor Axel Kicillof, who is considering running against Milei, has denounced the plan on social media platform X, stating "Milei now wants to change the rules of democracy to improve his chances of reelection by cheating." articles.title: Breakthrough Discovery Made in Catalyst Development Using Molecular Cages
articles.summary: Researchers from top UK universities have developed a new method to identify highly effective artificial enzyme-like catalysts by combining machine learning with a rapid screening technique.
articles.content: A breakthrough discovery has been made by chemistry researchers using powerful "molecular cages" that mimic the behavior of nature's enzymes. These tiny, hollow structures can trap molecules and accelerate chemical reactions, much like miniature reaction chambers. The scientists have developed a new way to identify and understand highly effective artificial enzyme-like catalysts. Researchers from top UK universities have worked together on this project, combining machine learning with a rapid screening technique. This approach has enabled the team to evaluate 30 distinct palladium-based molecular cage structures in a single study, rather than preparing and testing each candidate individually. Professor Paul Lusby from the University of Edinburgh led the research, which involved assembling and assessing these molecular cages immediately in solution. This allowed for rapid assessment of their performance. The results showed enormous differences in performance among the catalysts. The best catalysts were found to be more than 10,000 times more active than the least effective ones. The study highlights a significant issue in catalyst development: the vast range of performance among molecular cage catalysts. Catalysts are crucial to modern manufacturing processes, accounting for approximately 90% of all chemical production worldwide, which includes essential products such as medicines, fuels, fertilizers, and plastics. A breakthrough method has been developed to accelerate the discovery of better catalytic cages by leveraging artificial intelligence and machine learning. This approach enables researchers to rapidly identify new catalysts that would otherwise be difficult to isolate and study. The experimental component of the study was led by Dr. Laura Bickerton, a postdoctoral researcher in Lusby's group, who utilized this method to investigate a wide range of molecular cages. Researchers used physically motivated features to describe the cages, including their shape, size, volume, and electrostatics, which were then analyzed using machine learning algorithms to understand why some cages performed much better than others. The research identified key design principles that enable molecular cage catalysts to perform optimally. These principles can be used to create more efficient catalysts, which are crucial for industries striving for sustainability and net-zero emissions in sectors such as pharmaceuticals, agrochemicals, and advanced materials. By applying these principles, researchers can design better-performing catalysts with reduced energy consumption and waste production. This approach supports the development of more effective chemical processes. The findings provide a new route to designing molecular cage catalysts efficiently, paving the way for innovative solutions in various industries.
